claims.text: The baseline is an equiatomic nanoscale solid-solution catalyst containing Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os.
The intervention increases Rh by approximately 10% relative to its equiatomic amount while decreasing Ru or another constituent to maintain the total composition.
Increasing Rh alters the local active-site electronic structure and local d-band center.
Changing the local electronic structure shifts the adsorption-energy distribution of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Rh enrichment shifts the adsorption-energy distribution toward a more optimal range.
Intermediates that bind too strongly poison catalytic sites.
Intermediates that bind too weakly lead to incomplete ethanol oxidation.
Optimizing intermediate binding through Rh enrichment favors a multi-electron ethanol-oxidation pathway approaching a 12-electron process.
IrOsPtPdRhRu can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
Rh enrichment enhances ethanol-oxidation activity relative to the equiatomic catalyst.
The Rh-enriched catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the equiatomic catalyst.
The Rh-enriched catalyst will have a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the equiatomic catalyst.
The hypothesis is intended to apply under alkaline or aqueous ethanol-oxidation conditions at moderate temperatures and active reaction potentials.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to nanoscale, homogeneous solid-solution particles.
Composition changes substantially beyond approximately 10% or conditions that induce phase segregation may fall outside the applicable regime.
The magnitude of the adsorption-energy change and catalytic-activity improvement is uncertain without targeted calibration.
The response to Rh enrichment may depend on pH, temperature, and electrolyte composition.

The hypothesis is falsified if Rh enrichment produces neither a statistically significant activity improvement nor the expected shift toward the 12-electron product pathway relative to the equiatomic control.
